content: The 2017 guideline titled Protecting, Promoting, and Supporting Breastfeeding in Facilities Providing Maternity and Newborn Services was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to provide evidence-based recommendations for improving breastfeeding practices in healthcare facilities. This guideline updates and replaces the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding outlined in a 1989 joint statement by WHO and UNICEF. It also complements other breastfeeding-related initiatives, such as the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) and the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. The guideline emphasizes the critical role of breastfeeding in improving child survival, nutrition, development, and maternal health. It aligns with global health goals, including the Sustainable Development Goals and the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition, which aim to increase the rate of exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months to at least 50% by 2025. The recommendations focus on specific practices that can be implemented in maternity and newborn care facilities to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. These include immediate support for initiating and establishing breastfeeding, addressing feeding practices and the additional needs of infants, and creating an enabling environment for breastfeeding. The development of this guideline followed rigorous procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. Evidence was gathered from systematic reviews, including 22 Cochrane reviews, to assess the impact of interventions on breastfeeding rates, nutrition, and health outcomes. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to high, depending on the intervention and outcomes assessed. Additionally, qualitative evidence was synthesized to evaluate the values, preferences, and acceptability of interventions among mothers and healthcare workers. The guideline is intended for policymakers, healthcare providers, program staff, and other stakeholders involved in designing and implementing breastfeeding support programs. It aims to inform evidence-based decisions to improve breastfeeding practices and outcomes in healthcare facilities. However, it does not provide comprehensive guidance on community-based breastfeeding support, workplace breastfeeding policies, or the full scope of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. WHO acknowledges the contributions of various experts, organizations, and donors, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Nutrition International, and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the development of this guideline. The recommendations were finalized during a meeting in Florence, Italy, in November 2016, with input from technical experts and peer reviewers. This guideline serves as a resource for improving breastfeeding practices in healthcare facilities and complements other WHO and UNICEF initiatives aimed at enhancing maternal and child health globally.
